records.title: LOCKDOWN
records.en: A 20-day survival game about cooking for a family in lockdown
records.abstract: LockDown is a survival game set in one apartment during a 20-day city lockdown. Each morning a supply package arrives, and by Day 7 it may be just noodles, a cabbage and rice. Cooking is a tangram puzzle: you cut the ingredients, fit them into a pan that is too small, and store the leftovers in a fridge where food rots. The family and the neighbours reach you through the phone. Based on my family's lockdown in Shanghai in 2022.
findings: Twelve ingredients, each a shape of 3 to 7 cells, are cut and fitted into a pan of 18 to 25 cells.
The fridge is a 6 by 8 grid. From Day 8, food stored for two days starts to rot, and the rot spreads to neighbouring cells.

The phone has a newspaper, a building group chat and a family chat. On Day 4 the building asks about medicine, on Day 5 the paper reports refills running late, and the same morning Grandpa's box is empty.

gallery.caption: Cut ingredients going into the pan

study.pitch: In LockDown the player lives in a small apartment with Grandpa and Daughter during a city lockdown. Each ingredient is a shape, and the pan is a grid that is always a little too small for the food. The game is twenty days long, but the player is never told that.

sections.heading: Where it started
body: In 2022 my family was locked down in Shanghai. There were five of us in the apartment: my grandparents, my parents and me. We ate what came in the government supply package, and some of the food had already gone bad when it reached us. My grandparents needed their medicine, and nobody was allowed out to buy it.
My parents kept the house running like that for months. The hardest thing was that nobody could tell us when it would end.

media.title: The package
media.note: We couldn't go shopping, so the player can't either. Each morning they get what is in the bag at the door and have to cook with that.

media.title: Grandpa's tablets
media.note: On Day 5 Grandpa's medicine runs out. His health drops every day he goes without it, and a better meal doesn't change that.

media.title: No end date
media.note: The screen shows the day number and how everyone in the family is doing. It never shows how many days are left.

sections.heading: One day
body: I want the player to feel how boring the lockdown was, so they do almost the same things every day. The mechanics that come in later are only small changes to what is already there, and the main thing the player does is still cooking the meal.

media.title: The package
media.note: A bag arrives at the door in the morning. The player doesn't choose what is in it.

media.title: One meal
media.note: The player fits the food into one pan for the whole family. What is left over goes into the fridge or is thrown away.

media.title: The table
media.note: The family eats and says what they think of it. Everyone's health and morale go up or down.

media.title: The phone, then sleep
media.note: Messages from the family and the building come in on the phone. Sleeping starts the next day, and nothing is reset.

sections.heading: The first version
body: I finished the first version in July. It ran for thirty days, and anything that had been in the fridge for three days simply disappeared. That was too simple. The player only had to remember which day the food went in.

Now rot starts in one cell of an ingredient and spreads to the cells next to it, and it can move into other food that is touching it. The player has to look at the fridge and decide what to cook first and what to move away.
I also cut the run from thirty days to twenty, and I rebuilt the room and the interface. The pictures show how the game looked in September, before that.

media.caption: The apartment, with a pixelated city behind it
The pan was a plain square
The fridge
The family chat on Day 5

sections.heading: The pan
body: The cooking puzzle comes from tangram, the Chinese puzzle where flat pieces have to fit inside an outline. In LockDown the pieces are ingredients and the outline is the pan.

A tangram has one correct answer. I didn't want that here, because there were no perfect meals during the lockdown. So every ingredient has a shape, calories and a food type, and there is never room for all of them. So the player has to choose which food to cook today and which to leave.

media.caption: Day 1. Pork, rice, tofu and cabbage are in the pan. The potato and the egg on the left didn't fit.
Tangram figures. Every one uses the same seven pieces.
Day 6
Day 8
Day 13
Day 19

sections.note: The pan has a different outline each day.

sections.heading: The knife
body: On Day 1 the handle comes off the family's knife, and for five days every ingredient goes into the pan whole. On Day 6 a new knife is at the bottom of the food bag. I use cutting to encourage the player to fit awkwardly shaped ingredients into pans that are a different shape every day.

The puzzle is my own version of tangram, the traditional Chinese puzzle. When I was thinking about how to add variations to it, I thought about what I really do when I cook: I cut food up, and I store some of it for later. Adding those brings my own life into the game. It also gives the player harder puzzles, and makes them think more about how to manage their food.

media.caption: Day 6. Cutting a piece of tofu in two before it goes into the pan.

sections.heading: The fridge
body: I made the fridge because during the lockdown we had to plan carefully too. We put some of our food away in the fridge to eat later, because we couldn't be sure what was coming. In the game the fridge is broken on Day 1, and Grandpa gets it working again on Day 3. It is a grid like the pan, and the leftovers have to fit in it.

In the game I made this harsher than it was for us. From Day 8 the building loses power at times, and the food in the fridge starts to rot. Rot spreads between cells that touch, and if rotten food goes into the pan, the family loses health. So every morning the player opens the fridge, cooks the oldest things first and drags the bad pieces away from the good ones.

media.caption: The fridge works again, and it is empty.
media.label: Day 3

media.caption: The dark cells are rotten: 13 of the 34 in use.
media.label: Day 8

sections.heading: The family and the building
body: There were five of us at home in 2022. In the game the family has three members, one for each age. Grandpa is old, and his health depends on medicine that has to come from outside. Daughter is young and says it out loud when she is hungry, bored or scared. The player is in the middle and does the cooking.

The neighbors are in the building's group chat, which comes from the residents' group our compound had. For it I picked four kinds of people who were typical of the lockdown. Director Zhang is the official one, who posts the notices. Aunt Li is the helpful one, who shares what she has. Mr. Wang is the pessimist, who doubts the notices and argues with them. The stranger on the sixth floor is the one who profits from the shortage, with medicine to trade for food.

media.caption: After each meal someone in the family says how it was.

sections.heading: The phone
body: In 2022 the news, our residents' group and my own family would all talk about the same shortage, and each of them said something different. So the phone in the game has the same three places to read: a newspaper, the building's group chat and the family chat.

Day 5 is an example. The newspaper says prescriptions are late all over the city. In the building group Aunt Li looks for her own box of tablets and finds it empty. In the family chat Grandpa says his are gone.
The newspaper never says when the lockdown will end. On Day 11 it reports that a reopening notice going around the chats was false.

media.caption: The newspaper.
media.label: Day 5

media.caption: The building group, after the player asks the neighbors for medicine.

sections.heading: Choices
body: Five of the twenty days have a choice. It comes as a chat message, and the player answers in the chat. Whichever answer the player picks, the family loses something.

On Day 5 Grandpa's tablets are gone. The player can ask the neighbors, which is free but may not work. They can send Director Zhang a photo of the empty box and wait for a pharmacy van. Or they can give two things from the fridge to the stranger on the sixth floor and get the medicine now.
The later choices are about food. A sealed floor asks for some, and Grandpa wants to give his share away.

media.caption: The last box of tablets is empty.
media.label: Day 5

media.caption: The seventh floor is sealed and asks for food.
media.label: Day 13

media.caption: Grandpa offers his portion to Daughter.
media.label: Day 16

sections.heading: The last morning
body: The lockdown ends after Day 20. Nothing in the game says it is coming, and the last day starts like all the others. Then the report comes up. It shows how many days the family spent at home and how healthy everyone is.
If anyone's health reaches zero, the run stops on that day and the same report comes up. I kept the report this short because I don't want the ending to feel like winning.

media.caption: The report after Day 20.
A run that stopped on Day 5. Grandpa's health reached zero.

sections.heading: How to play
body: Left mouse: click the floor to walk, click the package, the counter or the fridge to use it, drag food into the pan or the fridge.
Q and E: turn the camera. Tab: phone. R: rotate the piece. Right mouse: put a piece back, or throw food out of the fridge. Space: make the cut. Esc: close.

media.caption: Day 7 in the apartment.

controls.say: click the package, the counter or the fridge to use it
drag food into the pan or the fridge
put a piece back, or throw food out of the fridge

download.label: Windows build v0.1.0 (Google Drive). Unzip and run LockDown.exe.

records.title: Last Mile
records.en: A management game about a food-delivery station
records.abstract: You manage Lanting, a small food-delivery station, for ten days. Orders appear on a 3D map of the district as countdown pins, and you assign each one to a rider, a ground robot or a drone. Riders are paid per drop, and each of them needs money for something by a certain day. From Day 3 headquarters starts adding machines, and each one takes a rider's place on the roster.
findings: Every order is assigned by hand. The deadline is set from the fastest available courier, so a late order is usually the result of a dispatch decision.
Four riders each have one bill due on a set day, and an even share of the orders is just enough to cover it.
The district is a road graph based on Xujiahui, filled in by editor scripts. A headless test plays all ten days and checks that all 132 orders resolve.

gallery.caption: Orders as countdown pins over the city

study.pitch: Last Mile is a management game. The player runs Lanting Station, a food-delivery station in Shanghai, for ten days. Orders come in from the shops nearby, and for every order the player picks which rider takes it. There are four riders and they are paid for each delivery, so picking one of them also decides who earns money that day.

sections.heading: Where it started
body: When I was back in China for the summer, I kept seeing delivery riders cut across the road wherever they could, just to make the time limit on an order. And now in Jersey City, across the river from New York, I see a lot of Uber's delivery robots on the sidewalks.

So the first version was about the rules the riders work under. The player never gave an order to anyone. They set the base pay, the late fees and how many orders a rider could carry at once, and about thirty riders decided for themselves when to accept, rest or quit. It ended the way the game still ends, with an AI taking the player's job.
When I played it I felt a long way from the riders, and the game was boring. I had nothing to do with any of them, so when I replaced a rider with a machine I didn't care why.
So I cut the riders down to four and gave them names, and now the player gives every order to one of them by hand.

media.caption: From the plan I wrote for the first version. Step 2 is the player's whole job: sliders and policy cards.
media.label: September 10

media.caption: A week later. Four riders with names along the bottom, and the player chooses who takes order #1001. The game was still in Chinese.
media.label: September 17

sections.heading: Dispatch
body: The player spends most of the game on this screen. Time stops while an order is open, so there is no need to click the first name in a hurry.
The deadline is worked out from the fastest courier who could take the order. When that one is already out, the player has to send someone slower or let the order wait.
points: Orders. Each one is a paper slip with a countdown.
The same order on the map, with the time it has left.
Dispatch. Everyone who could take it, when they would arrive, and how early or late that is.
The roster. A card that can't take this order is locked and says why. The robot can't climb stairs.
The selected rider: Streets, Strength, Judgment and stamina.

media.caption: Day 4. A breakfast for the sixth floor of a building with no lift.

sections.heading: The four riders
body: With only four riders the player gets to know each one. They have three numbers out of ten, for how well they know the streets, how much they can carry, and how they handle a difficult handover. Each of them is also saving for one thing that has to be paid by a certain evening.

I set the amounts so that a fair share of the work just about covers them. A rider who is passed over for a few orders comes up short, and that stays for the rest of the run. Xiaoyu loses the room, moves an hour away, and is 20 seconds late to every shift after that. Chen leaves after day 9.

media.caption: Streets 9 · Strength 4 · Judgment 9
media.title: Chen
media.note: He has been on his route so long that his customers phone him and not the platform. He needs ¥80 for his wife's medicine by day 9.

media.caption: Streets 5 · Strength 9 · Judgment 5
media.title: Ajie
media.note: He carries the crates. The board counts a crate as one parcel, so he is last on it. He owes a friend ¥50 by day 6.

media.caption: Streets 8 · Strength 6 · Judgment 6
media.title: Lin
media.note: He has a daughter to pick up from school, and both times he calls it is about getting there. His rent, ¥40, is due on day 5.

media.caption: Streets 4 · Strength 6 · Judgment 8
media.title: Xiaoyu
media.note: She joins on day 2 and gets lost in the old blocks. The deposit on her room, ¥30, is due on day 4.

sections.heading: Pay
body: The platform pays the riders, and the station doesn't. A delivery is ¥4 to ¥6, and half of that if it is late. So when the player gives an order to one rider, the other three earn nothing from it.

On day 4 Xiaoyu texts during the evening wave. She is ¥30 short on her deposit, it is due tonight, and the order she is asking for pays ¥5. The player can give it to her, promise her the next one, or tell her not now. If the player promises and then gives someone else an order she could have taken, the promise is broken.

The report at the end of the day has the station's target and every rider's pay on one page. On this day the station delivered 12 against a target of 10. Xiaoyu took home ¥5, she is last on the board, and her deposit fell short.

media.caption: Day 4, evening. Xiaoyu asks for order #1007.
The report that night.

sections.heading: During the shift
body: A shift gets interrupted a lot. All of these used to open as the same box in the middle of the screen. I moved each kind onto its own object, so the player can see what kind of thing it is before reading it. The clock waits while one is open, and every answer has its cost written on the button.

media.title: An alert
media.note: News for the whole station drops down under the header. On day 4 it starts to rain and every courier except the drone slows down.

media.title: A ticket
media.note: Between the two waves a ticket prints with the plan for the evening: keep it standard, pay ¥40 for more time, or take rush money and tighter deadlines.

media.title: The walkie-talkie
media.note: A courier who is stuck on the road calls in. Here the customer has moved the drop-off and Ajie is circling the block with a crate of milk.

media.title: The phone
media.note: A rider who wants something texts. The phone sits at the right so the map stays in view. Lin is asking to skip the rush and pick up his daughter.

sections.heading: Story calls
body: From day 2, one rider calls each evening about something the board doesn't count. Ajie wants a day off the crates. Lin wants to finish early for school pickup. Chen wants someone to learn his route. Yes usually costs ¥30 and about 25 seconds of the rider's time, and no is free.

The calls follow on from each other. Xiaoyu has three. On day 3 she asks if someone could ride the old blocks with her once. On day 7 head office has asked her to mark the entrances the robots keep getting wrong, and she asks for a little time to write them up properly and for the notes to say they are hers. On day 10 she asks if her name is going in with the final report.
The robots use her entrances in the end even if the player says no. Her name is only kept on them if the player says yes.

media.caption: Day 7. Xiaoyu asks for time to write up the entrances, and for her name on them.
The player says yes, and she answers.
AO-6 files it.

sections.heading: Robots and drones
body: On day 3 head office sends a robot on trial and wants it compared with the riders by the evening. If the riders were on time more often, the player can send it back. If they weren't, it stays, and the player either pays to keep everyone or lets one rider go.

I didn't want the machines to be riders with better numbers. The robot never gets tired and isn't paid by the delivery, but it can't climb stairs or check an ID at the door. The drone is the fastest thing on the map, but it can't lift a crate. So in the first days the station still needs riders for those orders.
Then head office asks for two machines on the roster, then three, then four. The roster only has six places, so to bring in a machine the player has to take a rider off.

media.caption: Day 3, after closing. The robot was on time more often, so it stays.
Day 7. The roster is full, so another machine means choosing who it replaces. Chen is selected.
The roster on day 10 of the same run: four robots and two drones.

sections.heading: AO-6
body: AO-6 arrives on day 6. For each order it marks one courier as its pick and gives a reason. The reason is usually one of the player's own earlier choices, with the day and the order number.

Every dispatch the player confirms is kept as an example, and so is every time they pick someone else. The newer examples count for more, and the next suggestion for that kind of order leans the same way.

I made AO-6 polite, and its picks are usually right. It never decides for the player. But its pick is at the top of the list and Confirm is the biggest button on the panel, so the easiest thing to do is agree with it. I wanted the player to train it by their own choice, without the game forcing them to.

media.caption: Day 6, 06:00. AO-6's first morning message, where Zhou Heng's used to be.
Day 8. AO-6 picks robot R-03 for a crate of milk: "This follows what you did on Day 7, #1082."

sections.heading: Day 11
body: Day 10 ends with a report and a thank-you. At 06:00 on day 11 the phone has a notice from head office. The manager's position has been removed and AO-6 runs Lanting now.

At first this was only a notice, and all the player could do was read it. So I let them answer back. They can ask AO-6 why, and it answers with the numbers from their own run: how many of its picks they confirmed, and how many calls from the road they handled. Then it lists the rules it took from them.
After that the title screen is different. The badge doesn't open the door, and there is a stamp on the shutter.
sections.note: There is one way off this route. If the riders beat the robot on day 3 and the player sends it back, the station stays all-human and AO-6 never arrives. The manager keeps the job if more than 80% of the orders from day 6 to day 10 are on time.

media.caption: The player asks who trained it. AO-6 answers with their own numbers.

sections.heading: The desk and the phone
body: The screen is the part I redid the most. The early versions looked like a dashboard. The version in the game now is made of things from the station manager's desk. Orders are paper slips with a tear line, and riders are ID cards in a rail along the bottom.

Between shifts the game is a phone. The morning message, the plan for the day and the evening report are all on it, and so is the notice on day 11. The light on the city changes from morning to evening, and the paper keeps its own colors so it reads the same at any hour.

media.caption: Dark panels over a dark city.
media.label: September 17

media.caption: Light panels, numbered like a form.
media.label: October 3

media.caption: The morning of day 4, on the phone.
media.label: Now

sections.heading: How to play
body: Left mouse: click an order, then a courier, then Confirm. Space: pause and resume. W, A, S, D: move the map. Drag the map with the mouse, and zoom with the wheel.
Esc: close the order. F8: fast forward.

media.caption: The city after dark.

controls.say: click an order, then a courier, then Confirm

records.title: Trail Adventure
records.en: A first-person climbing and wildlife photography game
records.abstract: You inherit a cabin and a camera from Leo, an old photographer, on a mountain island with 24 animal species. Each trip starts by packing four tools at the cabin bench and ends at the summit, or when hunger, cold and tiredness have eaten the stamina bar. Any slope over 50 degrees can be climbed. Sixteen islanders ask for photos and send tools back by paper parachute.
findings: Climbing, running and jumping all spend one stamina bar. Hunger, cold, tiredness, injury and pack weight each shorten it.
A photo scores one to three stars from what is in the frame: distance, eye contact, flight, young, golden hour. Each species has a list of moments to collect.
The island, cave and mine are built by editor scripts, and the UI is drawn in code to look like a paper journal.

gallery.caption: Creeping up on deer by the pond

study.pitch: Trail Adventure is a first-person game. The player climbs a mountain island with an old camera and takes photos of the animals that live there. Most of the playing time goes into climbing. I made each animal hard to get to, so that the player remembers the climb and not only the photo.

sections.heading: Where it started
body: I started hiking after I moved to the United States for university, and I usually had my camera with me. The game comes from those trips. Mount Rainier is the one I remember best. A ground squirrel sat on the rocks and looked straight at me. Higher up it was foggy, and a marmot was watching from a ridge. Both of them lived a long way up, and I only saw them because I had walked that far.

The basic rules of the game are taken from those trips. Animals stay away from the path, so the player has to climb to get to them. Climbing uses stamina. Animals leave once they notice the player, so a good photo usually takes patience.

media.caption: A ground squirrel on Mount Rainier, looking right at me
A dolphin off Tampa
Horseshoe Bend

sections.note: A few of my photos are in the game too. They are the first pages of Leo's Journal.

sections.heading: The first version
body: In the first version, the player followed a fixed trail with obstacles on it and rolled a die at each one to get past. I got this idea from real hiking, because on a real mountain you almost always stay on the trail. In the game, though, there was only walking between the obstacles, and it was boring.

While I was testing it, the part I enjoyed most was running around and taking photos of the animals. It also reminded me of Antelope Canyon in Arizona. When I was there I really wanted to leave the trail and walk out into the desert around it. So I decided to build the game around photography and let the player walk wherever they want.
I removed the trails and the dice. Now the player can climb anywhere on the mountain to look for animals, and the mountain is the obstacle.

media.caption: Trailhead
A collapsed bridge: use a rope, or roll 5+ to climb down
Rolling
Rolled a 2, -20 stamina

sections.note: October 11 build. I didn't take screenshots back then, so I checked out that version again and captured these.

sections.heading: Climbing and stamina
body: Climbing is slow on purpose, about 0.6 meters a second. The player goes up one pull at a time, following the hands. I kept the hands low on the screen so they don't cover the rock or an animal sitting on it.
Running, climbing and jumping all use stamina, but walking is free, so that the player can look at the mountain and not at the bar.

Hunger, cold, injury, tiredness and a heavy bag each take a piece off the end of the bar, and each piece has its own color. This idea comes from the game Peak. I like it because I don't have to explain several systems to the player. The stamina bar is the only resource they have to manage, and every other effect is added on top of it. It is also how a real hike works, where being hungry or cold just means you have less energy to climb, and I think that helps the player feel they are really on the mountain.

media.caption: Stamina bar at the Snow Fire, evening. Hunger and cold have each taken a slice.

sections.heading: Photography
body: In real life, animals get scared when a person shows up. But when they haven't noticed anyone, they carry on with their own things, and every animal has moments of its own that are worth a photo. The scoring follows this. A photo gets more points if the animal is close, if it is running or flying, or if it is looking into the lens.

When I take photos while running, they come out shaky. I also didn't want the player to run up to an animal and take a quick shot, so moving while shooting blurs the photo. A blurred photo only gets half the score and can't be sent for a request.

New photos earn stars, and the player spends the stars at the bench in the cabin to upgrade the camera. I wanted photography to have a positive feedback loop. The more good photos the player takes, the better the camera gets, and with a better camera they can take more and better photos.

media.caption: The viewfinder right after a shot.
Fitting a new lens at the camera bench.

sections.heading: Animals
body: The animals I met on real trips did not all react to me the same way. On Mount Rainier the ground squirrel sat and looked right at me, and the marmot kept watching from a ridge. So in the game all 24 species behave differently. When an animal notices the player, it might stare, freeze, ignore her or walk closer. When it gets scared, it might run, crouch, climb a tree or charge at her.

Some have habits of their own. Foxes steal snacks. Goats spar with each other and will butt anyone who gets too close. The ptarmigan hen won't leave her nest, and the owl is only out from early evening until morning. Sneaking lets the player get nearer before being noticed.

The field guide works like a Pokédex. Each animal has a list of moments to photograph, such as a close-up, on the run, or at night. Every new moment gives one star, so the player has a reason to go back to an animal they have already photographed.

media.caption: The fox's page in the field guide, with its moments listed.

sections.heading: Legendary creatures
body: When people are out in nature, they often feel that something like a mountain spirit might live there. I wanted the game to have that too, so the island has nine legendary creatures, taken from Chinese ink landscape paintings and old Chinese stories. They are very hard to find and hard to photograph well. Meeting one is a surprise, and it gives the player one more reason to keep climbing.

Six of them are inside paintings. The player touches a scroll, ink covers the screen, and when it clears she is standing inside the painting. Most of them come out of the mist to watch her, and go back into it if she gets too close.

The other three are in the sky. The Wind Whale circles the island over the sea all day. The Thunder Wyvern only appears after it starts raining, so the player has to pick a day with rain in the forecast.

media.caption: The Water Dragon, photographed inside its painting.
Concept painting for the Water Dragon's tarn.
The Branch Beast in its painting.

sections.heading: Requests
body: Sixteen people live on the island. Each one has a short story of two or three photo requests. The stories don't depend on each other, so getting stuck on a hard request only stops that one story. I spread the requests so that every one of the 24 species is asked for at least once, and this takes the player all over the island.

Every request gives an item back, and all eight tools come from requests. So every tool the player gets has a small story behind it, and it doesn't feel like something she just picked up off the ground.

The Flashlight is an example. The cave is completely dark inside. Nell stands at the cave mouth and won't go in. When the player talks to her, she says that someone else on the island, Shepherd Bram, has a flashlight. The player goes to find Bram and takes a few photos for him, and then he gives her the Flashlight. With it she can go back and explore the whole cave.

media.caption: Nell at the cave mouth.
Bram's last request: the ducks on the pond.
The ducks in the viewfinder.
The Flashlight comes down by parachute.
Down the mine ladder by flashlight.
Old Ida in the Miners' Camp.

sections.heading: The cabin
body: When I get home from a real trip, I have photos and a few small things from the way. The cabin is where the game keeps those. Every trip starts and ends here.
points: Camera bench. The player spends stars here to upgrade the camera.
Carver's Shelf. When every moment of a species is in the field guide, the player can order a carving of it.
Photo board. The player's favorite photos.
Postcard strings. When someone's story is finished, they send a postcard with a note on the back.
Wardrobe. The jackets hang here. Every tool has its own place in the cabin.
Packing bench. The player packs the bag here before a trip.

media.caption: The mail-order catalogue sells furniture and carvings for stars, so the camera is not the only thing stars can buy.

sections.heading: Planning a trip
body: Before a trip the player makes a few choices in the cabin. I put them there so that part of the day is already decided when she walks out of the door.

media.title: The weather
media.note: The window shows the weather for the day. If it says cold or rain, a jacket is worth a place in the bag.

media.title: Packing
media.note: The tools for the day are laid out on the bench by the door. Here the Flashlight is going on the trip.

media.title: Where to start
media.note: On the wall map the player picks the trailhead or any fire she reached on an earlier trip.

media.title: Film
media.note: One roll is ten shots, and a new roll only comes from resting at a fire. The number at the bottom right of the viewfinder is how many shots are left.

sections.heading: How to play
body: W A S D: walk. Shift: run. C: sneak.
Left mouse: hold on rock to climb. Space: jump, or lunge up while climbing.
Right mouse: raise the camera. Left mouse: take the photo. Scroll: zoom.
R: find animals nearby. E: talk, rest, use. Tab: phone, settings, quit. I: bag.

media.caption: The Wind Whale passing the mountain.

controls.say: jump, or lunge up while climbing

download.label: Windows build, 1 Nov 2026 (Google Drive). Unzip and run Trail Adventure.exe.

records.title: Sniff & Snitch
records.en: A two-player online co-op stealth game
records.abstract: Two players break out of a magic prison together, one as Lyra, a witch, and one as Fia, a red panda. Routes split where one of them can pass and the other can't, and doors, boxes and takedowns need both. Guards see in a 120-degree cone and hear through walls. A caught player is taken to a gas cage, and the partner has 15 seconds to open it. Capstone team project; I'm a programmer and designer on it.
findings: Guards are state machines with 18 states. They see 12.3 m in a 120-degree cone and hear through walls, with each wall halving a sound past its first 5 m.
A caught player is walked to a gas cage. The partner has 15 seconds to reach it and hold E for 1.5 seconds.
Doors, push boxes, the lift gate and the takedown need both players. The server only syncs who is gripping, tap counts and start times; animations are computed locally.

study.pitch: An online co-op stealth game for two. Lyra, a witch, and Fia, a red panda, break out of a magic prison together. I'm a programmer and designer on the capstone team, and I built the guard AI, the capture and rescue loop and most of the two-player mechanisms.

facts.label: Engine
facts.value: Unity 6, C#, Netcode for GameObjects, Unity Relay

sections.heading: Lyra and Fia
body: Lyra and Fia are both in for theft, and neither of them gets out of the prison alone. Each player claims one of them on the character select screen, and the run starts once both roles are taken.

We built the two of them to be good at different things. Lyra is 1.8 m tall, drags boxes, and can put on a mask that keeps guards from growing suspicious of her. Fia is 1.0 m tall, jumps 1.4 m to Lyra's 1.0, climbs ledges and can dash 3.5 m. Some magic barriers stop only one of them, marked with a paw or a witch icon, so most rooms have a route for each.

media.caption: Character select: each player picks a mugshot card.
Fia's mugshot card on the character select screen.

sections.summary: Each player picks one character and the run starts when both are taken. Lyra is 1.8 m tall, can drag boxes, and can wear a mask that stops guards getting suspicious. Fia is 1.0 m, jumps 1.4 m to Lyra's 1.0, climbs ledges and dashes 3.5 m. Some magic barriers only block one of them, marked with a paw or a witch icon, so most rooms have a separate route for each.

sections.heading: Meeting up
body: The first stretch of Level 1 gives Lyra and Fia a "Find a way out" step each. The two run in parallel, and only when both are done does the next step appear: "Meet at the door".

Each character also has an exit of their own, and the level is won only when both players are standing in theirs. A checkpoint saves only after every connected player has walked into it, so a restart always brings the two of them back to the same checkpoint.

media.caption: The success screen, shown when both players reach their exits.

sections.summary: The start of Level 1 gives each character their own "find a way out" objective. They run in parallel, and only when both are done does the next one appear: meet at the door. Each character also has their own exit, and the level is only complete when both are standing in theirs. Checkpoints save when every connected player has reached them.

sections.heading: Guards
body: I built the guard AI. Each guard is one state machine with 18 states and a suspicion meter from 0 to 1. He sees 12.3 m in a 120 degree cone. An unmasked player within 2.8 m fills the meter in one second, and at the edge of his sight in about 1.8 seconds.

Hearing is a separate system. Crouching carries 4 m, walking 10 m and running 16 m. The first 5 m of a sound pass through walls at full strength, and each wall after that halves what is left, so Fia running behind one wall is heard out to 10.5 m instead of 16.

A noise can pull a guard off his patrol, but it cannot interrupt a guard who is already watching someone. I set it up this way so a thrown coin has to be planned before a guard looks at you; once he is watching, it does nothing.
sections.summary: I built the guard AI. Each guard is a state machine with 18 states and a suspicion meter. He sees 12.3 m in a 120-degree cone, and an unmasked player within 2.8 m fills the meter in a second. Hearing is separate: crouching carries 4 m, walking 10, running 16, and each wall past the first 5 m halves the sound. A noise can pull a guard off patrol but not off a player he is already watching.

sections.heading: The cage
body: Getting caught does not end the run. The guard cuffs the player and walks them to his cage. During the escort their camera sits 35 degrees off the guard's right shoulder, because from straight behind, the guard hides the player walking in front of him.

In the cage, green gas thickens as time runs down. The partner has 15 seconds to get there and hold E for 1.5 seconds. Opening the lock makes a 14 m noise, and for 20 seconds any guard who sees the empty cage comes to check. When Fia frees Lyra with the gas nearly full, the clang of the lock turns the nearest guard toward them as they run.

If the time runs out, or a guard catches the second player while the first is still held, the level ends for both. I built the cage HUD for the free player: a cage icon tracks the partner across the screen and flashes faster as time runs out.

media.caption: The game over screen when the partner is not rescued in time.
Fia's game over card: "You have been captured."

sections.summary: Being caught doesn't end the run. The guard cuffs you and walks you to his cage, where gas fills up over 15 seconds. Your partner has that long to reach the cage and hold E for 1.5 seconds. Opening the lock makes a 14 m noise, and for 20 seconds any guard who sees the empty cage comes to check. If time runs out, or the second player is caught too, the level ends for both.

sections.heading: Doors and boxes
body: The latch door has one lever locked to Lyra and one to Fia, and opens only while both are down. The push box has a handle for each at their own height. Once both have grabbed, either player's W fills one shared ring, and ten taps slide the box 2.5 m. Pushed off a ledge, it becomes a step, and the landing reaches guards 25 m away. The lift door is a heavy gate they raise together, walk under, and let slam shut behind them for good.

The takedown needs both players too. A masked Lyra presses a seal onto an unaware guard, which weakens him for 6 seconds. In that window Fia drops onto him from at least 1.4 m above, and he is out for 12 seconds unless another guard walks up and wakes him.

For these mechanisms the server writes only who is gripping, how many taps have landed and when a sequence starts. Each machine works out the door height and the players' animations from that start time, so a player who joins late sees the same door and no animation has to be sent.
sections.summary: The latch door has a lever for each character and opens only while both are held down. The push box has a handle at each height; once both have grabbed it, ten taps of W move it 2.5 m. For the takedown, a masked Lyra marks a guard, then Fia drops on him from above 1.4 m. The server only syncs who is gripping, how many taps have landed and when a sequence started. Each client computes the door height and the animations from that.

sections.heading: Pings and throws
body: Middle mouse drops a ping on whatever is under the crosshair. Each player has one ping at a time, and it lasts 8 seconds. A ping on a guard sticks to him and moves with him, so the partner knows which guard is meant after he turns a corner.

Holding E lifts a crate overhead. A tap of the left mouse button tosses it 4 m, and holding for half a second throws it 8 m. The crate sits a set height above each character's own head, because a height measured on Lyra left Fia's crate floating a metre above her.

A teammate set up the first quest data and HUD. I turned each level's quests into node graphs of reach, interact and acquire steps, each assigned to Lyra, Fia, either or both, with the server deciding who completed each step. Character select is server-owned as well, and a player who drops out mid-level rejoins in whichever role is free.
sections.summary: Middle mouse puts a ping on whatever is under the crosshair for 8 seconds, and a ping on a guard follows him. Holding E lifts a crate; a tap throws it 4 m, a half-second hold 8 m. The crate height is relative to each character, because a height set for Lyra left Fia's crate floating a metre above her head. I also rebuilt the quest system as node graphs of reach, interact and acquire steps, each assigned to Lyra, Fia, either or both.

sections.heading: Next
body: Coins still use an older flat noise radius that ignores walls, and I want them on the same hearing model as footsteps. Lyra and Fia have separate entries in the noise table with the same values, and quieter steps for Fia would give the players a reason to send her ahead.

Every guard has a hearing multiplier, set to 1 in the current levels; I want to use it for a guard dog at 2.5. I also built a slow curse for guards who cannot reach a player, which slows the player to 45% speed for 3.5 seconds, and I want to place it where a player can stand out of reach.
sections.summary: Coins still use a flat noise radius that ignores walls, and they should use the same hearing model as footsteps. Fia's footsteps should be quieter than Lyra's, to give a reason to send her ahead. Every guard has a hearing multiplier, currently 1, which I want to use for a guard dog at 2.5.
